issue.issue_text: Whether an accused not formally arrested at the time of giving information can be deemed to be in the ‘custody’ of the police for the purpose of admissibility of evidence under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, 1872.

facts: The appellant made a disclosure statement about the murder of his cousin while he was already detained by the police for a different case (the murder of his uncle).
He had not yet been formally arrested for his cousin's murder at the time of making the statement.
This disclosure statement led to the recovery of the deceased's body parts, which was used as evidence against him.
law: Section 27 of the Evidence Act is an exception to the general rule that confessions made to police are inadmissible (Sections 25 & 26).
It allows the part of a statement from a 'person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer' that leads to the discovery of a fact to be admitted as evidence.
application: The Court adopted a wide and pragmatic interpretation of the term 'custody', rejecting a narrow or formalistic view.
It held that 'custody' under Section 27 does not require a formal arrest. It includes any form of restriction, restraint, or even surveillance by the police.
The Court reasoned that as soon as a person's liberty is curtailed and they come into the hands of a police officer, they are considered to be in custody.
This broad interpretation is necessary to prevent police from evading the rules by simply delaying the filing of an FIR or a formal arrest.
The Court relied on the binding precedent set by a Constitution Bench in *State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyay*, which established this principle.

Applying this to the case, the Court found that since the appellant was already detained by the police in another case, he was under their restraint and therefore 'in custody' for the purposes of Section 27, making his disclosure statement admissible.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an accused does not need to be formally arrested to be considered 'in the custody' of the police for a statement to be admissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. The Court held that any form of police restraint or surveillance is sufficient to constitute custody, and therefore the appellant's disclosure statement was admissible.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellant under Sections 302 and 201 of the Penal Code, 1860 were justified.

facts: The appellant was convicted for murder under Section 302 and for causing the disappearance of evidence under Section 201 of the Indian Penal Code.
The dead body of the victim was recovered based on information known to the appellant.
In a separate case, the appellant had been acquitted of the murder of his uncle.
During his statement under Section 313 of the CrPC, the appellant denied all accusations but did not provide any explanation for his special knowledge of the location where the body was found.
law: Under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon them.
A statement under Section 313 of the CrPC allows the accused to personally explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against them.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principle of Section 106 of the Evidence Act, noting that the appellant had special knowledge regarding the place from which the dead body was recovered.
The Court found that the appellant's failure to offer any cogent explanation for this knowledge during his Section 313 statement led to a reasonable adverse inference against him.
This adverse inference was treated as an additional link in the chain of circumstantial evidence, which further affirmed the conclusion of his guilt based on the prosecution's evidence.

The Court also held that the appellant's acquittal in the separate murder case of his uncle was not relevant or of evidentiary value in the present case, as the conviction was sustainable based on the evidence on record for this specific crime.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction was justified. It upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the appeal, finding that the adverse inference drawn from the appellant's failure to explain his special knowledge, combined with other evidence, was sufficient to sustain the conviction.

appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that since he had not been formally arrested when he gave the information, he was not in police 'custody' as required by Section 27 of the Evidence Act. Therefore, the evidence discovered as a result of his statement was inadmissible.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that 'custody' for the purposes of Section 27 is not limited to formal arrest. A person can be deemed in custody if their movement is restricted and they are under the surveillance of the police, making the subsequent disclosure statement admissible. The text supports this by noting that the clause “accused of any offence” is descriptive of the person and does not require them to be formally accused at the time of making the statement.

A key argument was that the appellant's failure to offer any explanation for his special knowledge of the location of the dead body led to an adverse inference against him under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, forming an additional link in the chain of circumstances proving his guilt.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, the 'discovery of a fact' is not to be equated with the physical object produced; rather, it is the knowledge of the accused leading to the recovery of the object that is admissible. Such a discovery gives rise to two alternative hypotheses: (i) the accused deposited the item, which is incriminating, or (ii) the accused merely knew of its location, which is compatible with innocence. The court must analyze which hypothesis to accept based on the case's circumstances. Furthermore, reliance on Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not dilute the prosecution's burden of proof and only applies after the prosecution has established facts through circumstantial evidence.
obiter: Courts must be vigilant about the application of Section 27 to ensure the credibility of evidence, as the provision is vulnerable to abuse.

The evidentiary value attached to evidence produced under Section 27 cannot be codified or put in a straightjacket formula; it depends on the facts and circumstances of each case and requires a holistic and inferential appreciation of evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, once the prosecution has established a complete chain of circumstances pointing to the guilt of the accused, the failure of the accused to offer any explanation for facts specially within his knowledge, as per Section 106 of the Evidence Act, can be held against him as an additional link that reinforces the conclusion of guilt.
legal_tests_applied: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met: (i) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established; (ii) the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused, that is to say, they should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty; (iii) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency; and (v) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.

Section 106 of the Evidence Act comes into play when the prosecution has already established facts by way of circumstantial evidence, placing a burden on the accused to explain facts especially within his knowledge.

A distinction is to be drawn between an incomplete chain of circumstances and a circumstance arising after a chain is complete, where a false defence or explanation from the accused is found to be false, in which event the falsehood is added to reinforce the court's conclusion of guilt.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's conviction was upheld because the court found that the prosecution had successfully established a complete and conclusive chain of circumstantial evidence pointing to his guilt.

The appellant failed to offer any explanation for his special knowledge regarding the location of the dead body, which led the court to draw an adverse inference against him under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, forming an additional link in the chain of circumstances.

The appellant's argument that he was not in 'custody' for the purpose of Section 27 of the Evidence Act failed because the court accepted that 'custody' is not limited to formal arrest and can include situations where a person's movement is restricted and they are under police surveillance.
why_respondent_won: The respondent (prosecution) successfully proved the various links in the chain of circumstantial evidence, meeting the high standard required for such convictions.

The respondent successfully argued that the appellant's failure to explain his special knowledge of the body's location invoked Section 106 of the Evidence Act, creating an adverse inference that served as an additional circumstance proving guilt.
The respondent's argument that 'custody' under Section 27 of the Evidence Act is a broader concept than formal arrest was accepted, making the appellant's disclosure statement admissible.
policy_considerations: The court clarified that reliance on Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not dilute the fundamental burden of proof which always rests on the prosecution. Section 106 is not a tool to shift the initial burden, but rather comes into play only after the prosecution has first established a compelling case through circumstantial evidence.
